headline_hi: प्लास्टिक मुक्ति के लिए युवाओं की पहल
summary_en: School students around the world are working to tackle the plastic problem. In a school in Singapore, seventy-two thousand plastic items were used every year. Students took part in the Unplastify Challenge and introduced reusable lunchboxes. With this great initiative, they won first place in this competition. This campaign is designed for teenagers aged fifteen to sixteen. Over the past eight years, three thousand students from twenty-five countries have joined it. Together, these children have helped prevent seventy-two tons of plastic waste. Students in Chile prepared a natural alternative to plastic glitter. In Costa Rica, natural loofah was used instead of plastic sponges. In Türkiye, students found an alternative to plastic gloves for health centers. The mindset of these young children is truly making the environment plastic-free.

lead.title: Teenagers Worldwide Are Tackling the Plastics Crisis
lead.summary: W hen students in Singapore looked around their school cafeteria, they could see a problem shared all over the world: Single-use Styrofoam was ubiquitous. They soon learned that the school’s 2,000 students used 72,000 pieces of Styrofoam and other types of plastic every year. To find a solution, they joined the Unplastify Challenge , a global movement initiated by the Latin American social enterprise Unplastify and funded by the National Geographic Society, a nonprofit that seeks to foster environmental stewardship. What makes the program unique is its audience, design and scope. Teenagers, usually 15 to 16 years old, design and implement solutions to “unplastify” their schools, communities, neighborhoods and homes. In Singapore, the students decided to campaign for multi-use lunch boxes, winning them first place in the Unplastify Challenge 2026, the 12th such event of its kind. A garbage-strewn beach in Bali, Indonesia. Unless effective action is taken, it’s predicted that global plastic production will more than double over the next 15 years. Credit: Mariia Ploshikhina / Shutterstock In the eight years since it began, Unplastify has worked with over 3,000 students at 400 schools in 25 countries, mostly in Latin America, but also in Africa, Asia, North America and Europe. Together these students have come up with over 1,000 strategies, leading efforts to avoid an estimated 72 tons of plastic. In Chile, students have designed a biodegradable alternative to plastic glitter, thus avoiding four kilos of plastic in a single year. In Costa Rica, students have replaced plastic sponges with natural luffa. headline_hi: पहाड़ों के लिए बनी उड़ने वाली कार
headline_en: Flying car built for the mountains
summary_en: Very inspiring news has emerged from the Almora district of Uttarakhand. Ravi Tamta, a resident of Kafalikhan village, has built a flying car. People used to take hours on winding roads to reach hospitals in the mountains. Seeing this serious problem, Ravi thought of making a flying vehicle. Without any engineering degree, he learned from the internet and worked hard for thirteen years. He developed a prototype of an electric vehicle named Hapida Skynex. This special vehicle can take off and land directly vertically without a runway. In the month of August, its first successful test took place at the Army helipad in Almora. This electric vehicle flew successfully in the air for about one minute. Its main purpose is to deliver immediate help during medical emergencies in hilly areas. This unique invention by Ravi could save many precious lives in the future.

lead.title: ‘I Had No Engineering Degree’: Almora Mechanic’s Son Learnt From the Internet & Built a Flying Car
lead.summary: Flying cars are once again taking over the internet, with Tesla’s plans fuelling conversations about a future where people could travel through the air instead of sitting in traffic. But in Almora, Uttarakhand, an innovator has spent 13 years working towards a similar idea, driven by a problem much closer to home. Ravi Tamta grew up in the mountains of Kaflikhan village near Jageswar Dham, where reaching a hospital could mean hours on winding roads. He began wondering if there was another way to travel through the hills, one that did not depend on roads or require an airport. Inspired by the challenges of reaching hospitals in the hills, Ravi Tamta spent 13 years developing a flying vehicle that can take off and land vertically. Photograph: ( Zee News) That question led him to build HAPIDA SKYNeX, an electric flying vehicle prototype that can take off and land vertically. After years of experiments, the vehicle completed its maiden test flight in August, taking off from an army helipad in Almora and remaining airborne for nearly a minute. A mountain problem sparked the idea For people living in hilly regions, distance is not always measured in kilometres. Winding roads and difficult terrain can turn a relatively short journey into a long trip, particularly when someone needs medical attention. Tamta began exploring whether a flying vehicle could help people cover such distances faster. His idea was to develop a vehicle that could rise vertically, travel over difficult terrain, and land without needing a runway. View this post on Instagram A post shared by The Better India (@thebetterindia) The aim is to make air travel more accessible in hilly regions, particularly during medical emergencies and in areas that are difficult to reach by road. headline_hi: जर्मनी में बनी सबसे ऊंची विंड टरबाइन
headline_en: Tallest wind turbine built in Germany
summary_en: The world's tallest wind turbine is fully ready in Germany. This giant turbine has been installed in Schipkau, eastern Germany. The height of the blade reaches up to three hundred sixty-five meters from the ground. At such a height, wind speed remains very fast and continuous. According to the company, it can generate nearly twice as much electricity as a normal turbine. Its initial capacity has been set at three point eight megawatts. Its rotor hub rotates at an impressive height of three hundred meters above the ground. A special telescopic tower technology was adopted to construct at such a height. It will be installed right above the existing wind farm like a second story. The company's founder, Jochen Grossmann, called it a big dream of his team. Its formal operation starting in November will give new momentum to clean energy.
source: The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News

lead.title: World’s tallest wind turbine reaches 1,197 feet in Germany
lead.summary: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM The world’s tallest wind turbine just reached full height in Germany. GICON ‘s pilot turbine in Schipkau, eastern Germany, now stands 365 meters (1,197 feet) tall from base to blade tip, making it Germany’s second-tallest structure after Berlin’s TV tower . Official commissioning is set for November. Higher altitude, stronger winds Higher up, winds are faster and more reliable. That translates to more hours of generation per year, and GICON says its design could produce roughly twice the electricity of a conventional turbine with the same rotor diameter. One thing to flag: that’s a claim about cumulative generation over time, not rated power. The turbine’s rated capacity is 3.8 megawatts; future versions are designed to go past seven. The rotor hub sits 300 meters (984 feet) above the ground. Building that high required rethinking construction. A crane capable of reaching 1,197 feet wasn’t realistic, so GICON used a telescoping tower instead. A specialized lifting system raised an inner tower through a surrounding lattice structure, then locked it at full extension. “365 meters – this is an overwhelming moment for our entire team,” said GICON founder and CEO Jochen Großmann. “What was long a challenging idea and then an equally challenging construction project now stands as a globally unique facility in Schipkau.” A second tier for existing wind farms GICON and its funder, Germany’s Federal Agency for Disruptive Innovation (SPRIND), aren’t pitching these turbines as replacements for existing wind farms. headline_hi: पर्यावरण अनुकूल मूर्तियों से नदी की सुरक्षा
headline_en: Protecting the river with eco-friendly idols
summary_en: Sculptors from the Kumartuli area of Kolkata have come forward to protect the environment. Sculptor Kaushik Ghosh is making idols using entirely natural materials in his workshop. Leaving aside thermocol and chemical colors, he has returned to his old traditional art. Bamboo, wood, jute rope, and clay are used in the making of these idols. For decoration, he chose the pith of the shola plant and natural colors. Every year after Durga Puja, thousands of idols are immersed in the Hooghly River. In the year two thousand twenty-five, around fifty-two hundred idols were immersed across thirty-four ghats. The river water was heavily polluted by floating waste of thermocol and plastic. Volunteers cleaning the riverbanks faced immense trouble gathering this trash. With Kaushik Ghosh's new thinking, our sacred Hooghly River will remain clean and safe. This initiative shows that both tradition and the environment can be respected together.

lead.title: ‘Thermocol Out, Clay & Shola In’: These Kolkata Artisans’ Durga Idols Won’t Choke the Hooghly This Pujo
lead.summary: At Joy Durga Bhandar, a workshop in north Kolkata's Kumartuli, Koushik Ghosh begins an idol with a framework of bamboo and wood tied together with jute rope. From this base come the sculpted figures, decorations and layers of colour that devotees see during Durga Puja. Koushik knows this process well. For generations, artisans in Kumartuli have worked with bamboo, straw and clay, shaping idols by hand for Kolkata's Durga Puja celebrations. Over time, many workshops also adopted thermocol decorations, synthetic paints and plastic ornaments because they were quicker or cheaper to use. Koushik is looking for ways to bring more traditional materials back into his work. "The frame, the clay, the straw, those were always ours. The thermocol and the chemical colours came later, because they were cheaper and faster. I am going back to what was here before," he says. The straw framework gives the idol its shape before artisans add the first layers of clay.   He is working towards idols decorated with natural clay, shola (the soft pith of a plant used for delicate ornaments) and natural colours instead of thermocol. Every year, after Durga Puja, thousands of idols are immersed in the Hooghly River and other water bodies. In 2025, around 5,200 idols were immersed across 34 major Hooghly ghats and approximately 30 other water bodies in Kolkata and nearby suburbs, according to The Times of India . Civic workers clear debris from immersion sites, but thermocol and plastic decorations need careful collection and disposal because they can persist in the environment. headline_en: New technique for acrylic glass recycling
summary_en: Scientists at ETH Zurich in Switzerland have achieved a major breakthrough in plastic recycling. Scientists have found a very simple way to make acrylic glass like new again. In the market, it is commonly known as Plexiglas. This transparent glass is found in our home windows, car lights, and furniture. Earlier, recycling this strong material was considered very difficult and expensive. The research team has developed a new and effective low-energy-consuming technology. This technology breaks down acrylic glass almost completely into its original chemicals. Through this, completely high-quality new material can be produced again from the same old material. This new discovery will make the reuse of plastic waste possible at a very low cost. This work by scientists will prove helpful in reducing plastic pollution worldwide.

lead.title: Scientists Discover a Simple, Low-Energy Way to Recycle Acrylic Glass into Brand-New Material
lead.summary: Researchers at ETH Zurich have found a practical new method that breaks down acrylic glass—known by the brand name Plexiglas—almost entirely into its original building blocks, making high-quality recycling realistic and affordable for the first time. Acrylic glass shows up in everyday products like windows, car taillights, furniture, and protective barriers. headline_hi: दीवारों पर काई उगाने वाला कंक्रीट
headline_en: Concrete that grows moss on walls
summary_en: A startup from the Netherlands has discovered a unique technique to turn walls green. This company, named Respyre, has created a special coating material called Mosscrete. This technology is based on research by scientists from Delft University of Technology. With the help of this coating, green moss grows easily on concrete walls. It does not require soil or any watering pipes. The moss absorbs moisture from the air and rain, spreading without damaging the wall. Its successful test was conducted on the wall of a large warehouse in Kortrijk, Belgium. At the same time, it was also applied to a sound barrier wall built in Hoofddorp, Netherlands. Compared to traditional green walls, it incurs no maintenance costs. This discovery will make the plain cement walls of our cities clean and beautiful.
source: The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News

lead.title: A Dutch startup is making concrete that grows its own moss
lead.summary: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Most building materials are designed to resist the elements, to stay sealed and unchanged for as long as possible. Respyre , a Dutch startup, is working from the opposite premise. The company has developed Mosscrete , a bioreceptive concrete coating that creates conditions for moss to grow directly on vertical surfaces, drawing moisture from rain and air without any soil or irrigation system. The science comes from research at Delft University of Technology , and since its commercial launch, Respyre has applied the technology across eight projects in Belgium and the Netherlands. How moss takes hold Moss doesn’t have roots in the conventional sense; it attaches to surfaces through rhizoids, tiny thread-like structures that cling to the material without penetrating or damaging it. Unlike a traditional green wall , which needs structural support for soil, a built-in watering system, and regular upkeep, Mosscrete sidesteps most of that. And because it’s applied as a coating rather than built in, it can go onto an existing facade just as easily as a new one. The material works especially well on blank or inaccessible walls where conventional planting isn’t an option, and Respyre has been using those spaces to test how the technology holds up under different real-world conditions. Eight buildings, different tests In Kortrijk, Belgium, 450 square meters (about 4,840 square feet) of a new industrial warehouse facade were coated with Mosscrete during construction and integrated with rainwater harvesting, keeping the whole system maintenance-free from day one. headline_hi: मंगल के चंद्रमा की ओर जापानी मिशन
summary_en: Japan has taken a big and remarkable step in the field of planetary science. On October nineteenth, Japan successfully launched a spacecraft. This craft is heading toward the mysterious moons of Mars. This mission is known as Martian Moons eXploration, or MMX. This spacecraft has departed from Tanegashima Space. The main objective of this mission is to collect soil samples from Mars's moons. After this, the spacecraft will bring these samples back to Earth. This will be the first time in history that a mission brings soil from a Martian moon to Earth. This is an extremely important step in taking planetary science forward.
